title: Data Types
summary: A data type tells Python what kind of value it is using, such as text, a whole number or a list.
introduction: A data type tells Python what kind of value it is using, such as text, a whole number or a list. Sort a few values into kinds. Then try changing a text number into a real number before doing maths with it.
learningObjectives: Identify the type of any value with type() and isinstance()
Convert between str, int, float and bool safely
Explain what dynamic and strong typing mean for your code
Recognise the collection types list, tuple, dict and set

blocks.text: Ask Python what something is with the built-in `type()` function. The four types you will use in nearly every program are `int` (whole numbers), `float` (numbers with a decimal point), `str` (text) and `bool` (`True` or `False`). `None` is a special value meaning *no value*, with its own type `NoneType`.

blocks.title: check_types.py
blocks.code:
print(type(42))
print(type(3.14))
print(type("hello"))
print(type(True))
print(type(None))

age = 30
print(isinstance(age, int))

blocks.text: `type()` returns the class itself, which is why it prints as `<class 'int'>`. When code needs to test a type, prefer `isinstance(value, int)` over comparing `type()` results: it reads better and also accepts subclasses, which matters once you write your own classes.

rows: Text of any length, including empty
Absence of a value, missing results

blocks.text: Python is **dynamically typed**: a variable gets its type from the value currently assigned, and you may assign a value of another type later. It is also **strongly typed**: Python never silently converts one type into another to make an operation work. JavaScript turns `"3" + 4` into `"34"`; Python raises an error instead, because adding text to a number is ambiguous.

blocks.title: python strong.py
blocks.content:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/ada/projects/strong.py", line 2, in <module>
    total = count + 4
            ~~~~~~^~~
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

blocks.text: The message says exactly what went wrong: you tried to concatenate (join) a string with something that is not a string, and the markers point at the `+`. Dynamic typing means errors like this appear when the line *runs*, not when the file is loaded, so a program can work for minutes and then fail on a path you never tested.
Conversion is explicit: call the type you want as a function. `int()` and `float()` parse text, `str()` turns anything into text, and `int()` applied to a float drops the fractional part.

blocks.title: convert.py
blocks.code:
count = int("3")
print(count + 4)

price = float("19.99")
print(price * 2)

print("Total: " + str(count * 10))

print(int(7.9))          # truncates towards zero, does not round
print(float(7))
print(int(True), int(False))

blocks.text: `input()` always returns a string, so the classic beginner bug is to add or compare the raw input. Convert it first, then calculate. In the output, `29` is what the user typed.

blocks.title: age.py
blocks.code:
age = int(input("How old are you? "))
print("Next year you will be", age + 1)

blocks.title: python age.py
blocks.content:
How old are you? 29
Next year you will be 30

blocks.title: Not every string converts
blocks.text: `int("3.7")` raises `ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '3.7'`, and so do `int("ten")` and `int("")`. Only text that looks like a whole number converts with `int()`; use `float()` for decimals, and when the text comes from a user or a file, expect failure and handle it, as shown in [Errors and Exceptions](/tutorials/python/errors-exceptions).

`bool()` converts any value to `True` or `False`, and an `if` statement applies the same rule implicitly. The falsy values are `False`, `None`, zero of any numeric type (`0`, `0.0`) and empty containers (`""`, `[]`, `()`, `{}`, `set()`). Everything else is truthy, including the string `"False"` and the list `[0]`, because a non-empty container is not empty.

blocks.title: truthy.py
blocks.code:
print(bool(0), bool(42), bool(-1))
print(bool(""), bool("False"))
print(bool([]), bool([0]))
print(bool(None))

blocks.title: python truthy.py
blocks.content:
False True True
False True
False True
False

blocks.text: Python's four built-in collections each get a dedicated lesson later; for now, learn to recognise their brackets. Square brackets make a list, parentheses a tuple, curly braces with colons a dict, and curly braces without colons a set.

blocks.title: containers.py
blocks.code:
scores = [90, 85, 77]              # list: ordered, changeable
point = (3, 4)                     # tuple: ordered, fixed
user = {"name": "Ada", "age": 36}  # dict: keys to values
tags = {"python", "beginner"}      # set: unique, unordered

print(type(scores), len(scores))
print(type(point), point[0])
print(type(user), user["name"])
print(type(tags), "python" in tags)

blocks.text: Indexing starts at zero, so `point[0]` is the first item. Strings are sequences too: `"Python"[0]` is `"P"`, as the [Strings](/tutorials/python/strings) lesson shows next.

blocks.title: Type hints
blocks.text: Modern code often reads `def area(width: float, height: float) -> float:`. Those annotations are *hints* for editors and type checkers such as mypy; Python itself does not enforce them at run time. The [Functions](/tutorials/python/functions) lesson shows where they belong.

questions.question: What type does `input()` return when the user types `42`?
questions.explanation: `input()` always returns `str`. Convert with `int()` or `float()` before doing arithmetic.
options: Whichever type matches what was typed

questions.question: `bool("False")` evaluates to `False`.
questions.explanation: Only the empty string is falsy. `"False"` has five characters, so it is truthy and `bool("False")` is `True`.

seo.title: Python Data Types – int, float, str, bool and None
seo.description: Learn Python's built-in data types, check them with type() and isinstance(), convert between str, int and float, and understand truthiness and strong typing.
